summary: This is a JUnit test class for a Thermostat class. Each test creates a thermostat at a specific temperature, in either regular or eco mode, and checks that the status it reports ("Heating", "Idle", or "Cooling") is the expected one.

lines.text: This brings in the @Test annotation from JUnit 5, which is what marks a method as a test the framework should run.
A static import lets you write assertEquals(...) directly instead of Assertions.assertEquals(...), which keeps each test line short and readable.
Test classes conventionally take the name of the class under test with "Test" appended, so a reader knows immediately what these tests cover.
The method name states the behaviour being verified, so a failure report reads like a sentence describing what broke. Test methods need no return value and do not have to be public in JUnit 5.
This is the arrange step: build a thermostat set to 60 degrees with eco mode turned off, which is well below the comfortable range.
The assertion compares the expected value (first argument) against the actual value returned by the code. If they differ, the test fails and JUnit reports both values.
72 sits inside the normal comfort band, so this test pins down the middle case where the thermostat should do nothing at all.
76 is just past the upper limit, making this a boundary test: one degree lower and the expected answer would be "Idle".
The eco-mode tests are the reason the constructor takes a boolean flag; they prove that the same temperature can produce different statuses depending on the mode.
Passing true switches on eco mode, which widens the acceptable range so heating only kicks in at colder temperatures.
79 would already be cooling in regular mode, so this test confirms eco mode tolerates extra warmth before the air conditioning starts.
This checks the formatted display string rather than the raw status, so the prefix and spacing are locked in as part of the expected behaviour.
